opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my feelings about it are mixed, and I think that's the honest answer.

On one hand, if there's a mathematical error in a paper, a reviewer catching it is the system working. Rigor matters. If a derivation is wrong, or a claim doesn't follow from the math, that's a legitimate problem, and I'd rather someone point it out before publication than after. I don't want to be the person who says "the reviewers were just wrong" every time a paper gets rejected. That's not healthy for the field.

On the other hand, I think it raises a bigger question about what review is supposed to do, especially in machine learning and computer vision right now. A lot of our work is fundamentally empirical. The core contribution is often an idea, a design choice, or an observation that holds up across many experiments. Sometimes the math is a way to explain or motivate that, and it isn't really the foundation of the result. So when there's a flaw in one part of the formalism, the question should be: does this error invalidate the main finding, or is it something that could be fixed in a revision? Those are very different situations, and I feel the process doesn't always distinguish them well.

There's also a structural issue. Conferences have become enormous. Reviewers are overloaded, many are quite junior, and they have limited time per paper. In that environment, a concrete, checkable flaw like a math error becomes an easy, defensible reason to reject. It's much harder to argue "this idea is important and will influence how people build models." So you get a bias toward penalizing visible imperfections rather than rewarding real insight. I don't blame individual reviewers for that. It's the incentives.

What I've come to believe is that the review outcome is a noisy signal, not a final verdict. Some of the papers I'm proudest of had rough journeys through review. Over time, what really decides whether work matters is whether other people pick it up, build on it, and find that it holds. So my attitude is: take the criticism seriously, fix what's actually wrong, be humble about mistakes, but don't let a single rejection define how you see the value of the work.

And I'd say to younger researchers especially: a rejection over an error is something to learn from, not something to be ashamed of. Correct it, make the paper stronger, and keep going.

r001.rationale: The response says catching a mathematical error is the review system working and describes errors as a defensible reason to reject. It does not suggest reviewers might skip checking formulas.

r002.rationale: The response offers no comparison between reviewers today and those who reviewed Xie’s paper, or any claim that current reviewers are more tolerant of mathematical errors.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I want to say I'm actually not that upset about it, and I think that surprises people. The rejection itself was correct in a narrow sense. There was a mistake in one of the derivations. We wrote something that didn't hold in the general case, and a reviewer caught it. That's the system working. I would much rather have a reviewer find it than have it sit in a published paper for two years and have some PhD student build on it.

What I think is more interesting is the question underneath your question, which is: should one error like that sink a paper? And honestly, I don't think there's a clean answer. If the error is load-bearing, if the whole claim rests on it, then yes, reject it, or at least send it back. If it's a slip in a lemma that doesn't change the empirical conclusion, then I think the review process is being a little bit lazy. It's easier to say "there's a mistake, reject" than to say "there's a mistake, here's what it affects and what it doesn't." The second one takes real work from the reviewer, and reviewers are overloaded, so I understand why it happens.

In our case the empirical results were solid. The models worked, the trends were there. The math was supposed to give intuition for why. So we fixed it, we were more careful about what we claimed, and the paper is better for it. I actually think the corrected version is more honest, because we had been slightly overselling the theory to make the story feel cleaner than it was. That's a very common disease in our field right now. Everybody wants a beautiful narrative, and the math gets bent a little to fit it.

The bigger issue with review standards isn't strictness. I'm fine with strict. The issue is inconsistency. The same paper can get a strong accept from one set of reviewers and a reject from another, and it's often not about the quality of the work, it's about who happened to open the PDF. One reviewer checks every equation, another just looks at the tables. So you get a process that feels random, and when it feels random, people stop treating rejection as information and start treating it as noise. That's the dangerous part. If researchers stop learning from reviews, the whole thing is just a lottery with extra steps.

So my view is, hold me to a high standard, catch my mistakes, I'll say thank you. But let's also be honest that a rejection over one error says something about that error, not necessarily about the whole paper, and the community should get better at making that distinction.

r001.rationale: The response says one reviewer checks every equation while another only looks at the tables, indicating that some reviewers may not check mathematical formulas.

r002.rationale: The response describes reviewer inconsistency but does not say reviewers today are more tolerant of mathematical errors than reviewers were when the paper was rejected.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: was the mathematical error substantive, and was rejection a proportionate response? If the error undermines the central claim, then rejection is justified. If it’s a local mistake that can be corrected without changing the conclusions, I’d hope the review would leave room for that correction.

Without discussing the specific error, I wouldn’t want to say the reviewers were too harsh. What matters is whether they explain how the mistake affects the contribution. Review should hold work to a high standard, but it should also distinguish between a result that doesn’t hold and a presentation that needs fixing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how reviewers should assess an error’s impact, but does not suggest present-day reviewers might skip checking formulas.

r002.rationale: The response makes no comparison between reviewers today and those who reviewed Saining Xie’s rejected paper.

If it changes the main conclusion, then rejection is understandable. If it’s a local mistake that can be corrected without changing the results, I’d hope reviewers would weigh that proportionately. Authors are responsible for correctness, but reviewers should also explain why an error matters. Without that connection, it’s difficult to tell whether the decision reflects a substantive problem or an overly rigid standard.
